I'm surprised they beat us at Go before Starcraft.

Go is much easier to play out mathematicly.

This SC2 ai is running off of the same knowledge a human player could have, unlike the games integrated bots.

The ai has to consider much more information compared to GO and make more meta-decisions like scouting, build order, race match-up etc.

While there is a lot of room for creativity of strategy in Go (which prevented it from being won by computers for so long), there is a lot more in most RTS games. The number of possible positions for a unit to occupy on top of considerations for dividing your forces and micro/macro management just make it all the more difficult to solve using the same tactics which had an AI winning chess (ie, calculating every possible future board state).

Add that to the fact that RTS's have hidden information in them as a genre trope (fog of war) and it makes the job of an RTS AI more about emulating the things a good player would do than about optimizing your next move to bring about the best possible game state.

It will probably take a different approach in order to produce a killer AI for something like Starcraft. If you use the same tactic that the Go AI used (pitting a neural network against itself until it knows so much about the game that it can win in any situation), an initial misconception about the full range of moves that the AI is allowed to make may limit its growth. It will be very good at fighting itself, but totally useless against a player. There may be an answer to the AI's strategy which is obvious to a player but inconceivable for the AI due to initial i/o assumptions. For their desired goal of beating international tournament winners, they will probably need to get the thing training off of actual players at the highest level of play. That Go was solved by this tactic is more statement of how comparatively limited the strategy options are between the two games.

Just my $0.02.
